Warping, judged by eye: 29 effects, one fix

Second category of the by-eye pass, picked because you had not named one. Every Warping effect is rendered by the app on the photograph its browser tile already uses, three ways: as shipped, with its main slider at a quarter, and at the top. This time each tile was rendered at your phone's real frame size (1080 px) and scaled down, because a 10 px displacement is 7% of a small tile and under 1% of a real frame; judged small, every pixel-based effect reads seven times too strong. The number on each tile is how far it moved the picture.

  • 29 effects on one photograph
  • 1 fix, shipped
  • 4 zeros that are not faults

The fix

Chromatic Aberration fixed in v15.83

Its description has always said "colour fringing toward the edges, the way a real lens misfocuses each colour". What it did was shift every pixel by one vector, which is exactly RGB Split, and the two rendered the same picture at their defaults. So there were two effects in the list with one look.

Now it has a Toward edges control, on by default: no fringe at the centre, growing to the corners, with Angle still steering the direction. Projects saved before this keep their old uniform shift exactly. Left: as shot. Middle: as it was. Right: now.

Zeros that are not faults

Four rows read zero somewhere on the sheet, each for a reason that holds.

Mirror, Shockwave, Wrap Shift

Zero at the top of the slider only: Mirror at position 100% puts the seam on the edge, Shockwave's ring has travelled out of the frame, and Wrap Shift at a full wrap is the same picture. A position, a moment and a period, not strengths.

Squish

Zero at every setting on a still, full-frame photograph, because it is a wall-collision effect: a layer sliding off-frame squashes against the edge, as its description says. Nothing here slides, so nothing squashes.

Everything else

Alive across the whole slider, and the ceilings raised last week (Wave 720, Ripple 480, Tile Rotate 1600, Pinch/Bulge 4) still change the picture at the top. Pinch/Bulge and Fisheye at their maximum magnify the centre so far that the source pixels show as blocks; that is what a fivefold magnification of a photograph looks like, not a defect.
